items.abstract: Moving beyond economic analyses of degrowth, growth and consumption are reframed through decomposition as a vital process through which life, value, and politics are continually re-composed. Against dominant imaginaries that cast decay as waste or ruination, this article turns to composting and carrion ecologies to articulate decomposition as a generative undoing and a mode of transformation that binds waste to worth. Drawing on multispecies examples from vultures in India to the Baltimore Compost Collective, the article situates decomposition as both material process and political metaphor to enact a revaluation of growth, decay, and consumption that unsettles capitalist logics of extraction and accumulation. It traces how practices of decay can cultivate livability and collective flourishing in the very sites marked by abandonment and disgust. In doing so, it challenges growth’s moral hegemony, recasts the ‘de-’ of decline, decay, and decomposition as a source of ecological vitality, and re-embeds growth within more-than-human cycles of breakdown and flourishing.
items.title: Rethinking (De)growth: the politics of compost

items.abstract: This article analyses discourses on artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of existential risk studies. AI appears as a key theme in existential risk circles, not only as a source of risk, but also as a resource for risk prevention and as the enabler of a glorious future for humanity. However, what is it about AI that brings together utopian and dystopian imaginaries? Why is a discourse on AI so tied to questions regarding the human, and what forms of humanity does it produce? What forms of governing does it enable? This article argues that the concept of ‘intelligence’ is fundamental regarding both how AI is construed as an existential risk, as well as how humanity is conceptualised as that which needs to be protected. Existential risk discourses on AI appear as a governmental rationality which reproduces exclusionary conceptions of humanity, as intelligence is mobilised as grounds for teleological conceptions of history and technological development, utilitarian ethics, and concerns for the long-term future. Consequently, existential risk prevention appears as a governmentality that mobilises uncertainty and the future of intelligence as ethical grounds for disciplining the co
items.title: The subject of intelligence: AI as existential risk and the government of the human and the future

items.abstract: Public discourse about polarisation has become one of the latest hypes in politics, whether it is in the political sphere proper, the media, or academia. Much like the populist hype and anti-populist discourse that preceded it, this phenomenon has prompted some interesting and useful developments in understanding our reactionary context. However, it also risks obscuring certain trends by mislabelling them as polarisation. One consequence has been found in demands for a return to post-political technocratic management with a focus on ‘concrete issues’ and public policies. This, it is argued, will move the focus away from divisive and irrational demands by the ‘extremes’ and restore order. This article contends that this ‘polarisation narrative’ simplifies complex issues through a bad analogy: the construction of a spectrum where good should be found in the middle of diametrically opposed political positions. To address this, we develop a critique of this narrative and highlight its limitations by examining democracy, political parties, and political participation in the public sphere. Subsequently, in response to the diagnoses and proposals of the polarisation narrative, this articl

items.abstract: Struggles for postcolonial restitution of heritage objects held in museums and other knowledge institutions in the west have challenged the legal and regulatory frameworks securing the collections’ integrity and unseizability and they have oppugned the epistemological power dynamics that manifest through the re-semanticization of the acquisitioned and confiscated objects as ‘mere things’. Drawing attention to the contrast between the international legal discourse of cultural property and what I call ‘refractory speech acts’ deployed by activists, artists and spokespersons from Indigenous communities within restitutive justice movements, I turn to political theories of Roberto Esposito and of Achille Mbembe to outline the critique of the epistemological power of western museums through the conceptual rubric of the ‘dispositif of a thing’ and to explore the possibilities for counter-action and alternative (non-Eurocentric and non-anthropocentric) understandings emerging through restitutive struggles today. Ultimately, I argue that the language, art and political action instantiated by these struggles are decolonizing practices that challenge the binary separation between persons and
items.title: Reframing restitution with Roberto Esposito and Achille Mbembe: restitutive justice struggles and the colonial ‘dispositif of a thing’

items.abstract: What, if anything, is new about the ethical demands that the Anthropocene places on human action? We refer to this question as the Anthropocene question, since only an ethics that provides a precise answer to that question is properly an ethics of the Anthropocene. While scholars in the environmental humanities have addressed the Anthropocene question, we bring this question to normative theory. To this end, we put forward a critical reading of Hans Jonas’s 1979 The Imperative of Responsibility , in which he develops normative principles on the basis of a historical diagnosis of novelty. Recent developments in scholarship on 5th-century B.C.E. Athenian tragedy allows us to challenge Jonas, who at crucial points misdiagnoses and overstates this novelty. Using Jonas’s work as an exemplar of a complete ethics of the Anthropocene, we highlight the importance of principles for ethical deliberation: an ethics for the Anthropocene needs not only principles for action, but also principles for how to deliberate on action. Criticizing Jonas’s and more recent views that democracy is unfit for the Anthropocene, we show that 5th-century Athenian tragedy was a sophisticated democratic practice o
items.title: Hans Jonas and Sophocles on the ethics of the Anthropocene

items.abstract: In a historical present marked by the ascendance of neo-authoritarianisms across the world, we bear witness to a renewed politics of hatred and violence and the heightening of the vulnerability of life. In this context, vulnerability has either been weaponised to justify violent forms of government or critically mobilised to stake a claim for justice, thereby becoming the object of political dispute. Against this backdrop, I explore this neo-authoritarian moment as one that enacts a political aesthetics of cruelty. This political aesthetics, I argue, points to the political capture of a death drive, that is, an inclination to destruction which has made itself available to social mobilisation through the normalisation of murderous hatred and political violence pivoting around the idealisation of sovereignty. In this vein, I examine vulnerability as a concept that foregrounds the relational character of our existence while illuminating the psychic register of relationality that challenges the drive to sovereign mastery and the sovereign self. Ultimately, I ask whether, and under what terms, those instances that invoke the relational dimension of bodily vulnerability can indeed challe
items.title: The political aesthetics of cruelty: contemporary authoritarian politics and the struggle between sovereignty and relationality

items.abstract: Intersectional theory has been criticised for neglecting religion and for being unable to account for religion’s social complexities. This contribution interrogates this critique by disaggregating different relationships of Muslim women to secular and religious varieties of patriarchy. We argue that what demarcates the challenges of intersectional analysis are the political contestations not around religion, but around women’s pro-patriarchal agency. We do so by discussing intersectional theory’s analytical usefulness and limitations in conceptualising the experiences of Muslim women. We focus on two interrelated dimensions: Muslim women in relation to secular patriarchy, and Muslim women in relation to religious patriarchy. We show that when analysed separately, the first dimension, the subjectivities of Muslim women in secular patriarchal spaces, do not pose a challenge to intersectional theory. We argue that intersectional theory’s limitations regarding the second dimension, Muslim women in relation to religious patriarchy, do not lie in its relation to Islam, but in its programmatic focus on problematising power inequalities. Lastly, in situating Muslim women at the intersectio
items.title: Is religion a problem for intersectional theory? Muslim women, feminism, and varieties of patriarchy

items.abstract: Nick Land is a British philosopher who has been leading the Dark Enlightenment movement. This paper examines the philosophical foundations of Land's right-wing trajectory and asks how the digital is integrated into his political economy and anti-humanist worldview. It situates Land within a broader context in which contemporary crises of neoliberal capitalism coincide with authoritarian and neo-reactionary currents often grouped under the label ‘Dark Enlightenment’. The analysis reconstructs continuities between Land's early work and his post-2013 writings by identifying five characteristic motifs that constitute the TOXIC schema, a mnemonic for the five key features of Nick Land's thought: T, the termination of Kant's influence; O, opposition to universalism and humanism; X, xeno-capitalism; I, informatic transhumanism; C, capitalist accelerationism. The paper analyses these five features. Land's position on capitalism as an autonomous, cybernetic, self-organising machinic system, based on Deleuze and Guattari's works, makes his work attractive to Silicon Valley gurus. His xeno-capitalism is a model for authoritarian statecraft (CEO-monarchy and ‘exit’ politics), while informatic
items.title: The TOXIC schema: How Nick Land's Dark Enlightenment works

items.abstract: Understanding how voters use the left-right scale is essential, as it is not only related to vote choice but also underpins how political scientists study ideology. This article finds that the way voters use the left-right scale is variable. Using British Election Study Internet Panel data from 2014 to 2024, I find that while economic and cultural values are both related to left-right self-placement, this varies both between individuals and over time. Those on the left of the self-placement scale can best be differentiated from one another by the strength of their economic values. For those on the right, cultural values are more useful in separating between different self-placement levels. Over time, left-right self-placement has become increasingly related to cultural values alongside economic values, driven by movements by people on both sides of the left-right scale. These findings indicate that even within one country, the meanings of ‘left’ and ‘right’ vary.
items.title: The changing meaning of left-right self-placement in the United Kingdom

items.abstract: Critics of neoliberalism increasingly examine its corrosive effects on democracy. Scholars often turn to Friedrich Hayek's political theory, arguing that it produces citizens who passively conform to spontaneous social orders. Yet insufficient attention has been paid to the normative conception of the human individual underlying his neoliberalism. This article demonstrates that Hayek's theory actively rejects individuality, understood as the cultivation and expression of one's distinct personal character. Individuality requires an experimental approach toward social action and critical reflection on whether social rules express one's character, yet such attitudes are systematically stifled in Hayek's account because they threaten the unequivocal obedience his spontaneous orders demand. My reading suggests that by suppressing individuality in favor of unreflective conformity, Hayek's neoliberalism produces citizens who are particularly ill‐equipped to identify and resist threats to their freedom and sustain liberal democracy.
items.title: Individualism Without Individuality: Friedrich Hayek and the Neoliberal Citizen

items.abstract: Social theorists in the Marxian tradition often interpret philosophical problems as reflections of social problems. This approach is central to Adorno's interpretation of Kant's epistemology. Adorno claims that the Critique of Pure Reason develops a concept of subjectivity that mirrors the “functionalization” of experience in capitalist societies. He retains that concept contradictory just as the social functionalism it ideologically reflects. In this paper I argue that Kant's concept of subjectivity is not contradictory and that Adorno must rely on it to articulate his critique of functionalism. Recognizing this Kantian debt implies not just acknowledging the Kantian sources of Adorno's model of ideology critique, but also revising central aspects of his social theory.
items.title: Adorno and the Kantian Sources of Ideology Critique

items.abstract: For the American Fourierist movement known as Associationism, the European revolutions of 1848 represented the opening scene of a new world-historical struggle: “the Emancipation of Labor.” The momentous example of the French Revolution in particular pushed this group of cooperative labor reformers, often dismissed as “utopians,” to embrace the politics and persuasiveness of working-class agitation as a tactical means to reorganize the system of industry. I argue that the Associationists—sidelined, when not forgotten, in the existing scholarship of “the American 1848”—should be appreciated for placing socialism on the agenda as the promise of a future workers’ democracy in the United States. Not only that, but they came to view the US labor movement itself as a participant in the social and political transformations of the 1848 revolutions. This is the Associationist 1848.
items.title: The Associationist 1848 and the Promise of Socialism

items.abstract: Does exposure to conflict displacement amplify support for far-right parties? This study investigates the political consequences of conflict-induced displacement in northern Israel by exploiting a natural experiment arising from government-ordered evacuations during military conflicts. Using a pre-registered survey and a regression discontinuity design based on an exogenous 5 km threshold, I assess changes in retrospective and prospective voting behavior as well as self-reported political ideology. The analysis reveals no evidence that displacement increases far-right support or induces partisan realignment. Rather, evacuees demonstrate a modest rightward shift in ideological self-placement without corresponding changes in voting behavior. This divergence suggests that displacement influences symbolic political positioning without prompting corresponding changes in voting behavior. These patterns unfold against a broader backdrop of political frustration and electoral disengagement that affects both displaced and non-displaced populations. The findings reveal troubling implications for democratic accountability during external conflict: leaders may be shielded from electoral conseq
items.title: Shifting sands? The impact of conflict displacement on voting

items.abstract: This essay is a response to David Lay Williams’ reading of Plato’s political thought, in his book The Greatest of All Plagues: How Economic Inequality Shaped Political Thought from Plato to Marx . The review essay asks three questions: Does Williams see among practitioners of contemporary political thinking any sign of a return to the deeper moral and philosophical aspects of political theory and any sign of a move toward expanding on the safer statistical approaches he himself diagnoses as insufficient? Of the two modes of responding to radical inequality, the imposition of practical impediments to acquiring massive wealth versus the re-education of the population toward an attitude that does not value the excessive accumulation of wealth, does Williams see across the canon of thinkers he treats here any general preference for one over the other? And lastly, in response to Plato’s apparent observation of a tendency in human life to lose sight of the whole of the political community one exists in and to focus on smaller horizons of concern, are there any strategies in Plato or in the other thinkers he treats, that Williams would suggest are valuable in combatting this tendency?
items.title: On Williams on Plato

items.abstract: This article challenges the reduction of blockchain to an institutional technology for lowering transaction costs by interpreting it as an autopoietic system of operational closure. Drawing on Francisco Varela's theory of biological autonomy and Cornelius Castoriadis’ account of political autonomy, it distinguishes between functional autonomy, understood as systemic self-maintenance, and political autonomy, understood as collective self-institution. The article argues that blockchain governance is marked by a rigidity paradox: the deterministic mechanisms that secure trustless coordination also risk foreclosing the indeterminacy required for democratic deliberation. Through the cases of the Ethereum hard fork and KONG Land, the article shows how algorithmic consensus can produce a form of functional sovereignty while displacing the interpretive and instituting dimensions of law. It concludes by proposing the need to rethink decentralized governance as an open rather than closed autopoiesis.
items.title: Algorithmic autopoiesis and the operational closure of law: The performativity of consensus as the production of socio-political reality

items.abstract: The American military–industrial complex is currently undergoing a profound transformation, recasting the triangle of political, military and corporate power anatomised by C. Wright Mills. Anchored in federally directed scientific research and a shared elite commitment to the geopolitical primacy of the militarised national state, the Cold War historical formation of the military–industrial complex was bound by a ‘military metaphysics’ that posited war as the era's defining necessity. This order has progressively unravelled with the shifting locus of technological development to the commercial sector. Pivoting away from the procurement process dominated by the defence primes during the War on Terror, the Pentagon has for the last decade courted Silicon Valley's tech giants and venture-backed start-ups in the pursuit of decisive military advantage amidst intensifying geopolitical competition. While the triangle's institutional orders persist, their hierarchy is now being inverted. Through its growing infrastructural power, ideological assertiveness and colonisation of political and military elites, a tech-capital pole is increasingly setting the terms for the whole. A new technologi
items.title: Inverting the triangle of power: The military–industrial complex after Silicon Valley

items.abstract: This article traces a single, three-stage argument. It begins by documenting, with empirical precision, how digital platforms functioned as genuine instruments of horizontal mobilization during the North African uprisings of 2010–2012. It then analyses how those same platforms were rapidly incorporated into new and frequently more sophisticated architectures of social control, transforming what had been emancipatory tools into what Foucault would call dispositifs of docility. Finally, it asks what theoretical apparatus is adequate to comprehend this transition—and argues that the most productive framework is a deliberate synthesis of Foucault’s analytics of biopower and disciplinary normalization with Bauman’s diagnosis of liquid modernity. The contribution of Bauman is not merely decorative: his account of how solid disciplinary confinement mutates under liquid conditions into consensual, self-administered surveillance explains precisely why the digital panopticon is so much more difficult to resist than its institutional predecessors. The article also examines the epistemological dimensions of this subjection, attending to the structural marginalization of non-Western knowledge t
items.title: The Architecture of Docility: Digital Platforms, Post-Revolutionary North Africa, and the Foucault–Bauman Dispositif

items.abstract: Contemporary critical theory elevates social norms to the status of positive knowledge and proclaims a politics of normative rightness to realise positive freedom and material equality in capitalist society. By accepting the positivity of norms, it fetishises them and prevents their denunciation, which alone exposes them. Based on the critical theories of Marx and Adorno, the article examines social norms as norms of a historically specific social content. In this process, the freedom of form is exposed in its content as the ‘freedom to starve’ (Adorno). Critique of exploitation does not call for normative arguments to understand its normative deficiencies with a view to achieving improvements. To understand the social norms, one must think in and through them to grasp their secret in the freedom of labour, which is the freedom of needy individuals to secure wage income. The circumstance that their prospects depend on the profitability of their labour connects the (promise of) freedom with exploitation.
items.title: Normative values and social critique: On Adorno and Marx

items.abstract: Neal Harris's Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies represents a significant contribution to the revival of first-generation Frankfurt School critical theory and its application to the contemporary alternative societies movement. This review essay evaluates Harris's central argument – that experimental pluralism among alternative societies is undermined by insufficient critique and an actionist displacement of strategic thinking – by placing it in dialogue with the existing scholarship on real utopias, workers’ cooperatives, mutual aid and universal basic income. The essay affirms the explanatory power of Harris's Frankfurt School framework, particularly his deployment of reification, instrumental rationality and repressive desublimation, while raising critical questions about the scope of the analysis, the tension between negativity and praxis and the risk of reproducing a specifically Western, male-centred theoretical horizon. The review ultimately endorses Harris's call for a renewed synthesis of critique and activism as an urgent priority for critical social theory.
items.title: Critique at the crossroads: On Neal Harris's Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies A review essay of Neal Harris (2026), Critical Theory and the Critique of Alternative Societies: Co-operatives, Mutual Aid and Universal Basic Income, Manchester: Manchester University Press, 254 pp. ISBN 978 1 5261 7222 8.

items.abstract: Contemporary diagnoses of resurgent authoritarianism frequently attribute it to the political mobilization of fear, drawing on a long tradition that casts fear as the antithesis of freedom. This article argues that such a framework is conceptually inadequate in the face of climate breakdown. It critically engages scholarship that cautions against environmental fear and catastrophist discourse, identifying three key assumptions underpinning most of these critiques: that environmental fears are politically homologous to other historically theorized forms of fear; that fear directly fosters authoritarian tendencies at the individual level; and that fear consolidates reactionary power while weakening emancipatory movements at the collective level. Against this affective determinism and threat functionalism, the article draws on ecofeminist and anti-militarist thought to reconceptualize fear not as a regressive affect opposed to democratic agency, but as an ambivalent, critical orientation toward shared vulnerability. In this context, affective self-defense emerges as key: a mode of political praxis grounded in the open, collective acknowledgement and articulation of fear - rather than
items.title: Reclaiming Fear in the Age of Climate Breakdown: From the Biopolitics of Catastrophe to Affective Self-Defense

items.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of sexual misrecognition: some groups are excluded from being seen as sexually desirable or are hypersexualised. This shapes their sexual subjectivity – how they understand themselves as sexual agents. Despite widespread initiatives calling for recognition in the domain of sexuality, the need for sexual recognition has remained undertheorised in recognition theory. Building on debates on the ambivalence of recognition, I argue that sexuality has a uniquely complex relationship to recognition. While sexual recognition is necessary for subjectivity, it also reinforces subjection to power structures. Moreover, sexuality continually transgresses sociality and subjectivity itself. Using Jeanette Chedda’s erotic story in Damn Horny as a case study, I demonstrate how sexual recognition transgresses ideals of mutuality and equality, and theorise transformative possibilities for cultivating sexual subjectivity differently.
items.title: The Ambivalence of Recognition in Sexual Subjectivity

items.abstract: This article offers a systematic and critical analysis of ordoliberal engagements with nature. Drawing on published and unpublished writings, private correspondence, and public addresses of key ordoliberal thinkers, primarily Alexander Rüstow and Wilhelm Röpke, it argues that their environmental thought was neither a precocious ecological awareness nor a coherent policy program, but rather a deeply romantic and conservative cultural critique of modern industrial society. Situating ordoliberalism within the broader intellectual milieu of Lebensphilosophie and the Conservative Revolution, the article traces how environmental ideas were embedded within their civilizational critique of modernity, functioning as a normative benchmark for social and cultural order. It further demonstrates how their conception of nature served to naturalize social hierarchy and legitimize a parochial vision of small-scale, locally embedded communities that proved increasingly difficult to reconcile with the economic realities they simultaneously promoted.
items.title: “Idyllischer Gartenzwergkapitalismus”: A Distinct Ordoliberal Environmental Framework?

items.abstract: This article critically explores council democracy as a utopian state order, on the basis of anarchist and Marxist works from western Europe and the United States, post-World War 2. As a system of national government, council democracy cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises. Collective self-rule cannot put an end to domination/hierarchy/rule but will engender another variety of ‘democratic hierarchy’. Comprehensive citizen participation locks citizens in an overregulated ‘democratic bureaucracy’, and delivers no feasible, working formula of government. In a paradox, council democracy is likely greatly to reduce the share of the population participating in the country’s political process, thus carrying less rather than more democratic legitimacy than representative democracy.
items.title: Collective Self-Rule and Comprehensive Participation: A Critique of Council Democracy

items.abstract: According to Adorno, all attempts to change society “immediately come up against the overwhelming force of inertia in the prevailing situation, and seem condemned to impotence.” This article explores the way the phenomenon of social and institutional inertia has been addressed in recent Critical Theory. It poses two central questions: firstly, what is social inertia, and what causes it? And secondly, how do we judge when institutions or social norms are “inert” or “obsolete”? It first briefly discusses the historical background of the problem of inertia, obsolescence and second nature in Hegel, Marx and the first generation of the Frankfurt School, and then discusses the central questions primarily with reference to recent work by Jaeggi and Menke and, to a lesser extent, Rosa and Von Redecker.
items.title: Social Inertia in Critical Theory

items.abstract: This review essay critically engages Andrew Hartman's Karl Marx in America , a reception history of three different classes of readings of Marx's writings in the United States. The essay's main contention is that Hartman's text, however unintentionally, seems to deviate from and thus challenges the anti-foundational principles that orient the genre of reception history. For, echoing Shakespeare's, Hegel's, and Marx's uses of the metaphor of the “Old Mole,” Hartman's own commitment to a labor-oriented version of “Marx”—from the three he charts in his topography of the Marx–America dialectic—works its way through Karl Marx in America , appearing at the end of text to subvert the groundless doctrines that guide reception histories.
items.title: “Well grubbed, old mole!”: On Karl Marx in America by Andrew Hartman, University of Chicago Press, 2025

items.abstract: This article examines how sustainability is rendered publicly legitimate in the current phase of green capitalism. Rather than treating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) as mere ideology or Solarpunk as external critique, it approaches both as modalities of public testing within a shared moral field. Drawing on Boltanski and Thévenot's sociology of justification, it argues that ecological legitimacy today is structured by a dominant normative test embedded in ESG discourse and a subordinate yet consequential sensible test, in which sustainability must also appear credible within shared perceptual horizons. To conceptualize this second dimension, the article introduces the notion of épreuve de sensibilité : a public test of rightness operating on the affective and aesthetic plane. Through a comparative analysis of European ESG regulatory texts (2019–2025) and a multilingual corpus of Solarpunk narratives (2012–2024), it shows how ecological morality is stabilized as procedural coherence in governance and staged as perceptual consonance in cultural imaginaries
items.title: Captured by the sun? Solarpunk, environmental, social, and governance criteria, and the pragmatics of green justification

items.abstract: In this text I reconstruct the thinking behind Althusser’s work to define philosophy, which culminated in his 1976 presentation at the Granada conference. I start by exploring how philosophy exploits and reorganises other forms of knowledge and social practices by means of an analysis of Althusser’s works in the later part of the 1960s. Subsequently, I examine and outline the debates on how the mode of production affects the superstructure. I then turn to the positions of Althusser’s interlocutor at the Granada conference, Juan Carlos Rodríguez, who defended the idea that philosophy was affected by the mode of production. Finally, I examine the implications of the changes and innovations in Althusserian thought set out at the conference for the conception of philosophy.
items.title: The Althusserian Transformation of Philosophy

items.abstract: Drawing on Heller’s sustained dialogue with Kant and Marx, the paper argues for the continuing relevance of her social philosophy while also foregrounding unexpected affinities between these two classic figures in their respective conceptions of social and political community. I first examine Heller’s interpretation of the Marxian ethical-political legacy, paying particular attention to social experiments such as the Paris Commune and their significance for a radical Enlightenment project that rethinks the relationship between state and society. I then inspect Heller’s engagement with Kant and Marx on the historical continuity of republicanism, highlighting the rejection of instrumental domination and the demand for symmetric reciprocity among social agents. Finally, I analyze Heller’s theory of needs, particularly the concept of “radical needs,” and argue for its relevance to contemporary debates on democracy, social reproduction and non-paternalistic forms of political organization.
items.title: From Marx to Kant: Social Domination and Emancipatory Praxis in Ágnes Heller

items.abstract: This article undertakes a historical-critical investigation of the intertwining of critical theory and functionalism in steps. It takes Adorno's critique of functionalism in architecture as a point of departure to distinguish the specific sense in which ‘functionalism’ is defined and subsequently rejected. The following section scrutinizes how critical theory deploys functionalist explanation, consciously or unconsciously, as the operative dynamic of its social diagnosis. On this basis, the third section utilises previously articulated methodological distinctions to outline critical theory's attempts at a normative reconstruction of the category of ‘function’. Then the inquiry pivots to the debates within analytical Marxism to examine critical theory's over-reliance on ‘objective teleology’ within its social diagnosis. Finally, the paper returns to the primary texts of sociological functionalism to refute critical theory's stereotype that equates function with end, thereby recovering more sophisticated understandings of functionalism for sociological analysis.
items.title: ‘Functionalist prejudice’: Critical theory and teleology

items.abstract: This article reevaluates Walling as a neglected precursor to American Western Marxism, arguing that his 1912–1914 trilogy synthesized Marxist theory of his time and Deweyan pragmatism into a distinct “pragmatist conception of history.” Born into “aristocracy” yet radicalized, Walling's unique trajectory—as a co‐founder of the NAACP and critic of Second International orthodoxy—shaped his approach: a rejection of deterministic scientific history in favor of instrumental, presentist analysis limited to recent generations. Although his work anticipated Western Marxism's cultural turn and superstructural focus, it also embodied tensions between materialist foundations and pragmatist subjectivity. Through critical engagement with Walling's contradictions—his Deweyan compromise, Nietzschean anti‐historicism, and idealist leanings—the article reveals the limits of his project. Ultimately, Walling's legacy lies in his paradoxical role: a bridge between Second International economism and later Marxist humanism, whose flaws illuminate broader challenges in adapting Marxism and its readings.
items.title: William E. Walling and the Pragmatist Foundations of Proto‐Western Marxism: A Re‐Evaluation and Critique

items.abstract: Habermas’ account of social identity is the most sophisticated among various deliberative and expansive democratic models and aligns with his long-standing theoretical commitment to communicative rationality that is tailored to the democratic organization of society. Taking a normative stance, he proposes a procedural account of social identity within communicative rationality, achievable only in modernity and deliberative democracy. We argue that his formulation of social identity is inadequate, given a problematic stage-based framework in his historical account of societal evolution and the insubstantial nature of social identity in his linguistic and procedural accounts of social identity. Nonetheless, Habermas’ approach can serve as a starting point to develop a more inclusive and empirically defensible conceptual framework for collective identity, grounded in robust institutional foundations and a substantive account of the political. Finally, by challenging Habermas’ separation of system and lifeworld, we argue that a rational social identity should be rooted in both domains.
items.title: Is it possible to form a rational identity? A critical reading of Habermas’ account of social identity

items.abstract: Recent scholarship has repeatedly highlighted a significant flaw in Giorgio Agamben’s Remnants of Auschwitz : its inability to account for acts of resistance in the Lager, or its aprioristic closure to the very possibility of such acts. As a result, instead of clarifying ‘the sense and reasons’ behind the behaviour of both executioners and victims of the Shoah, as his work initially sets out to do, Agamben’s analysis ends up rendering their conduct even more enigmatic and unintelligible. To address this lacuna in Agamben’s work, I draw on Foucault’s later studies on antiquity – precisely the so-called ‘ethical’ Foucault whom Agamben dismissed in favour of the ‘biopolitical’ Foucault. In doing so, I aim to bring to light a particular form of resistance described by Primo Levi in If This Is a Man : what he calls ‘moral survival’. Through this framework, I seek to partially reconstruct the rationality behind the conduct of those Häftlinge who, like Levi himself, attempted to resist the immanentizing pressure of the lex of the camp (i.e., the process of Muselmannization ) by constituting themselves as the ethical subjects of their own moral acts.
items.title: Beyond Agamben’s bare life: Understanding acts of resistance in the camp with Levi and the late Foucault

items.abstract: This essay explores the distinctive humanist method through which The Greatest of All Plagues investigates the presence of economic inequality in the history of political thought. It then follows the various thinkers in the book—from Plato to Marx—and observes that a vocabulary of virtue and wisdom not only accompanies but often underwrites criticisms of inequality deep into the 19th century. In conclusion, Williams’ book implicitly allows his readers to perceive how virtue ethics and criticisms of inequality have only become separated in the late modern period. In the 21st century, their rapprochement will deepen and energize inquiries into virtue ethics and egalitarian approaches to political economy alike.
items.title: Virtue, wisdom, and inequality: A response to David Lay Williams’ The Greatest of All Plagues

items.abstract: If Foucault was anything, he was a particularist. And yet, if we are to find valuable tools in his method today, they must be able to assist our framing and analysis of non‐particular issues. By what means can Foucault's methods grasp trans‐contextual problems? I investigate this question by reconsidering the status of power in Foucault's genealogical method. Rather than acting as an object of inquiry, I propose that power operates as an orienting analytical category at the level of Foucault's method. I make the case that conceiving of power in this way facilitates a substantial degree of generalization of his approach that he and his commentators have frequently been wary of claiming. This rethinking of power and method establishes the capacity for Foucaultian methods to address contemporary systemic and global problems.
items.title: The Purview of the Particular: Power and Method in Foucaultian Genealogy

items.abstract: : Using speculative fiction as a cultural probe, this essay critiques “deathbots” as extensions of late neoliberal capitalism. By examining Black Mirror , Upload , and The Final Cut , I make the case that these stories demonstrate a colonization of grief where the dead become extractable data for profit and the bereaved become dependent users. The essay draws on Homi Bhabha’s concept of mimicry and Sherry Turkle’s “ELIZA effect” to show how artificial intelligence simulacra trap mourners in loops of sycophantic affirmation that interfere with real grief. These technologies, I argue, foster a “crisis of narration,” the inability to achieve the temporal closure necessary to mark an end to grief and transform the raw data of loss into shared meaning. Ultimately, digital afterlives foster emotional stasis rather than healing, necessitating a critical recovery of memory and communal rituals in an era of algorithmic intimacy.
items.title: Digital Necromancy and the Fictional Imaginary: Speculative Probes into Deathbots and the Neoliberal Afterlife

items.abstract: This introduction to the special issue “What is Sedimentation? Consciousness, History, Language” clarifies the central role of sedimentation in Husserlian and post-Husserlian phenomenology and sets the stage for the essays that follow. Borrowed from geology, sedimentation functions in phenomenology as a concept-metaphor for the temporal layering of experience, habit, and meaning, linking static, genetic, and generative phenomenology. It names both the formation of a sedimented unconscious and the possibility of reactivation, thereby grounding phenomenological accounts of historicity, tradition, and critique. The introduction focuses on Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, Ricœur, Gadamer, and Derrida, while also indicating later reinterpretations in figures such as Stiegler and in political theory. It then presents the individual contributions, which explore sedimentation across embodiment, language, narrative, institutions, surprise, gesture, and psychopathology, showing how it conditions continuity while opening possibilities of transformation.
items.title: What is sedimentation?

items.abstract: As interstate cyberconflict intensifies, the intersection of national security, cybersecurity, and International Relations (IR) theory has emerged as a critical venue for scholarly inquiry. Yet due mainly to epistemological problems, IR theory has been limited in examining how it informs the maximization of strategic cyberpower and in testing key realist concepts and assumptions against cyberactualities, risking theoretical stagnation and conceptual infertility in the study of statecraft and cybersecurity. I seek to bridge these theory-testing and conceptual gaps by assessing offensive realism’s assumption about the scope of hegemonic expansion in cyberspace using the crucial case of the United States. I argue that offensive realism has meaningful explanatory and predictive power in cyberspace but sometimes lacks this power under conditions assumed by the theory, emphasizing the need to modify offensive realism’s understanding and scope conditions of hegemony. The US pursues global, not regional, cyberhegemony using offensive strategies to maximize its cyberpower for cybersecurity. Therefore, I critically examine defensive realism and cyber persistence theory as alternative structu
items.title: Great Power Cyberpolitics and Global Cyberhegemony

items.abstract: This article offers a critical phenomenological analysis of prevailing myths of menopause. By drawing on Simone de Beauvoir's conceptions of myths that essentialize existence, we have analyzed contemporary TV series in which menopause is portrayed. We identified the following myths of menopause: the myth of the liberated woman, the unnesting (s)mother, the old, ugly, and sexless witch, the mild, wise, and uncarnal woman. We first describe these myths and analyze how they may be interpreted as marginalizing in various and sometimes ambiguous ways. Then, we trace out two distinct ways in which some TV shows expose these myths as essentializing myths, which is important for allowing us to take a distance from them, and thereby to resist them. The first one is in line with what Beauvoir herself suggested as a fruitful dealing with myths: replacing mythical thinking with actual experiences. The second way is conceptualized on the basis of Irigaray’s thinking about mimicking myths. Such dealings with myths of menopause, we argue, may open the road to less marginalizing and more pluriform thinking about menopause.
items.title: Mimicking myths of menopause. A critical phenomenological perspective on ageing and femininity in fiction TV shows

items.abstract: Although it is well-known that Hannah Arendt gives a privileged role to action, her comments on the relationship between action and will(ing) have caused much confusion in the literature: commentators are split on whether her analysis of willing in The Human Condition (from 1958) and the essay “What is Freedom?” (from 1960) contradict or are complemented by her later analysis in The Life of the Mind (from 1978). I defend the latter position, but in contrast to others who have affirmed the same argument but focus on other themes to show it, I actually set out to show that Arendt offers a remarkably consistent analysis of the relationship between action and will(ing) throughout her work. To do so, I adopt a somewhat counterintuitive hermeneutical strategy by starting with her late analysis of will(ing) in The Life of the Mind (from 1978) where she most explicitly distinguishes between the historically dominant form of will(ing) of the liberium arbitrium and what I call natal-will(ing), before reading that distinction back into her earlier analyses of freedom in “What is Freedom?” (published in 1960), and action in The Human Condition (published in 1958). This hermeneutical strategy i
items.title: Arendt, free will, and action

items.abstract: This article considers a 2010 government report on the South African visual arts industry. Using a Foucauldian lens, I show how it produces a discourse on ‘gender’ and ‘race’ where these terms function only as quantitative and statistical categories in an administrative and economic art world model. The report presents its findings according to four figures, namely, the ‘white male’, ‘white female’, ‘black male’ and ‘black female’, which I conceptualize as knowledge ‘avatars’ acting as placeholders that obscure the field’s complexity. Despite the use of ‘gender’ and ‘race’ terms identifying various issues in the field, the report’s recommendations to the government virtually ignores the race/gender imbalance so clearly revealed – it is simply folded out of sight or performed away discursively. This phenomenon is explained via Jennifer Tennant Jackson’s concept ‘the efficacity of meta-conceptual performativity’ – how discourses can push things away from the regular knowledge surface (the dispositif ) into the ‘fold’.
items.title: The text folds: Disappearing race/gender in South African visual art world discourse

items.abstract: ‘Labour republicanism’ harnesses the ideal of freedom as nondomination to explain and challenge the injustices marring current workplace relations. Central to its challenge is a call for institutionalizing worker voice, with some also calling for workplace democratization and reorganizing capitalist enterprises along cooperative lines. Labour republicanism, in turn, has been criticized, most notably by the ‘commercial republican’ Robert S. Taylor. Taylor contends that contrary to its intentions, labour republicanism, or, more particularly, ‘radical labour republicanism’, would perpetuate domination by undermining freedom of occupational choice; enabling tyrannical workplace majority rule; concentrating too much power in state agents; and encouraging revolutionary violence and violent reaction from capitalist interests. To counter workplace domination, we should not institutionalize worker voice, but instead augment workers’ exit options through instituting a market-friendly property-owning democracy. This paper argues that Taylor errs in his claims against radical labour republicanism on account of distorting its implications for occupational choice and obscuring how freedom-as-non
items.title: Radical labour republicanism: A defence

items.abstract: Factionalism broadly describes the occurrence of conflicts between varying groups (or factions) within a social movement. Factionalism is often thought to be a negative feature of social movements. The goal of this paper is to (a) motivate the significance of the concept of factionalism for social and political philosophy and (b) give a definition of factionalism that captures the sense in which factionalism is a deep political problem. Specifically, the paper argues that factionalism is a form of anti-solidarity; factional groups are groups that, in virtue of their normal functionings, promote anti-solidaristic relations. Consequently, factionalism is particularly harmful because it has a transformative effect on movement actors: namely, it creates actors who are unwilling or unable to engage in collective political struggle. In a slogan: factionalism atomizes.
items.title: What Is Factionalism?

items.abstract: This response to critics addresses the questions raised throughout the symposium on the various issues raised throughout the Greatest of All Plagues . I address some of Cordelli's concerns about Hobbes's empirical assumptions by turning to Tocqueville. I answer Kirkland's questions regarding the nature of reforms intended to rectify inequality—whether practical or moral. Finally, I address Arlen's objections that the book has focused too much on the moral dimensions of inequality at the possible cost of underemphasizing the dangers of oligarchy. This particular concern provides an opportunity to discuss Walzer's Spheres of Justice and the difficulties of walling off inequality from other spheres of social life.
items.title: Response to critics

items.abstract: In an effort to manage carbon emissions, nitrogen runoffs, and other externalities, governments are increasingly resorting to a drastic policy measure: paying workers to stop working. Though such initiatives may be, strictly speaking, welfare enhancing, they are increasingly politicized, and often meet with protests. What explains public attitudes to “wage buyouts”? This article compares the explanatory power of two ideal-type theories in deriving a set of testable expectations. The first views work primarily as a means of earning a living; the second envisions it as a source of personal identity and social recognition. We test these opposing accounts using three survey experiments fielded on a combined sample of over 7,500 U.S. respondents. Overall, a sizeable portion of workers are resistant to being freed from work. Strikingly, individuals are more willing to reduce their work hours by half than to cease work entirely, even when offered full compensation. Those whose occupations are threatened by structural factors like offshoring or automation show lower identification with their jobs, and are accordingly more willing to accept government compensation for giving up those jobs.
items.title: On Paying Workers to Stop Working: Public Attitudes toward “Wage Buyouts”

items.abstract: Beliefs about the future shape attitudes, experiences, and priorities in the present. This article explores the relationship between democracy and the expected world to come. As it argues, visions of the future are an important resource for democratic politics, putting the present in critical perspective, aiding in the formation of a collective agent, and consolidating commitment in adversity. Indirectly, they contribute also to the legitimacy of democratic institutions, shaping the exercise of citizenship and the capacity to contend with the flaws of representation. The democratic significance of the imagined future becomes even more visible in today’s age of skepticism toward future-regarding politics, in which speculative modes of thinking run up against the desire for certainty and precision.
items.title: The Future as a Democratic Resource

items.abstract: Thomas Schelling’s 1966 classic, Arms and Influence , became one of the major strategic works of the Cold War, and it remains the clearest argument for the implicit logic of American and Russian coercive forms of diplomacy. Schelling is incisive about the credibility of deterrence, but the credibility of leadership is reduced to the Cold War assumption that power is decisive. While the rise of China and Putin’s invasion of Ukraine have rekindled interest in Schelling’s approach, the diffusion of agency and the interrelationship of issues in the current multinodal era have undermined the efficacy of hegemonic coercion. Rather than restoring Cold War bipolarity, the rise of China has created an asymmetric parity with the United States in which overlapping interdependencies inhibit the formation of camps. In the new era, the pursuit of strategic advantage by any state, large or small, must aim at securing its multidimensional welfare in a complex and unpredictable environment. The global powers are not hegemonic contenders, but rather the largest powers in a multinodal matrix of autonomous states in which each confronts uncertainty. A strategy based on coercion is likely to be less ef
items.title: Contra Schelling: The trap of Coercive Strategy in a Multinodal Era

items.abstract: One of the most prominent minority groups today is trans people. Those who see themselves as fighting for trans rights have tended to take these to include a right to legal recognition by the state, and social treatment by fellow citizens, as the sex of identification. These rights claims have been given substantial legal and institutional uptake. If trans people's full inclusion in public life requires legal recognition and social treatment as the sex of identification, then this is merely a description of things being as they should be. But if trans people's inclusion within the liberal state does not require these things, then this may be a description of a violation of liberal neutrality, the enforcement by the state of a contested and controversial conception of the good; and a tyranny of the majority, the weight of social opinion being pressed against those who want to talk about (what they see as) the fact that things are not as they should be. One way to gain some clarity on whether things are as they should be or not is to carefully consider the principles that liberal democratic states have used to secure the full inclusion in public life of other minority groups, and the
items.title: What Does Trans Inclusion in a Liberal State Require?

items.abstract: This conceptual-speculative article examines political polarization as a deliberate strategy of affective governance in an age defined by mass dispossession and ecological collapse. We argue that polarization should not be treated as a temporary crisis to be resolved but as a governing technology that organizes fragmentation, consolidates elite power, and deflects attention away from demands for structural transformation. To theorize this dynamic, we introduce the concept of affective eugenics , describing how affective governance legitimizes privatized futures for the few while rendering the many surplus through a sentimentalist and biopolitical sorting of affective capacity. Within education, this affective sorting materializes as a triage of feeling: elite institutions cultivate planetary crisis managers, middle-class students are conditioned for resilient compliance, and underfunded schools are left to manage disposability. We conclude by outlining the educational implications of affective eugenics and calling for praxes of affective de-settlement, refusal, and opacity that unsettle these hierarchies.
items.title: Affective Eugenics: Education, Political Polarization, and the Affective Sorting of Futurity

items.abstract: This article examines the institutional, technical, and ontological consequences of plagiarism detection platforms on contemporary academic writing. It argues that services like Turnitin and Grammarly do not simply detect plagiarism but actively reconfigure what counts as authorship, originality, and intellectual integrity. Drawing on historical and media-theoretical perspectives, the article traces plagiarism’s emergence as a culturally contingent offense, showing how its definition has shifted from oral cultures all the way to algorithmically processed patterns. In this transformation, plagiarism detection becomes less a neutral evaluative tool than a form of infrastructural governance that translates interpretive judgment into machinic legibility. Drawing on theorists such as Foucault, Chun, Kittler, Flusser, and Byung-Chul Han, the article situates plagiarism detection within a broader shift from expressive authorship to operational formatting. The article argues that plagiarism detection tools function as psychopolitical instruments, reshaping academic labor through anticipatory compliance and rendering originality as machinic compatibility.
items.title: Writing for Machines, Formatting Originality: Plagiarism Detection and the Automation of Authorship

items.abstract: Jacob Taubes’s book Occidental Eschatology (1947) offers a unique framework for examining cultural patterns across the line often construed as separating ‘the religious’ from the ‘non-religious’. This article highlights the implications of the application of this framework for our understanding of modernity: With Taubes, the ‘modern’ conception of history, totality and sovereignty can be traced to the emphatic distinction between ‘world’ and ‘God’ in the Hebrew Bible. In this perspective, ‘the modern’ appears as a cultural element that is analytically dissociated from any particular later historical period and from any cultural or geographical context, such as ‘the West’. Messianic thinking appears integral to the modern rather than as a source of fundamentally opposing insights. Competing appeals to reject the world are a source of instability and violence in modernity. Further research can address how the modern is linked with other cultural elements and with institutional arrangements in different contexts.
items.title: Rethinking the Modern and Modernity with Jacob Taubes

items.abstract: This article critically examines the ongoing debate about whether the British Empire was a force for good, exemplified by the recent exchange between Robert Tombs and Alan Lester, as well as Nigel Biggar’s defence in Imperial Reckoning . It highlights how defenders of imperialism use historical narratives to justify colonial atrocities and resist critique. It argues that imperialism’s legacy persists through three main forms. (1) Structural power and domination: the colonial project established entrenched systems of political, military, and economic control, justified by narratives that portrayed the West as morally superior. (2) Historiography and glorification: imperial defenders construct dominant histories that glorify empire, marginalize dissent, and present their perspective as objective truth and, in the process, silence alternative voices. (3) Contemporary cultural reconfigurations: modern imperialism manifests in culture wars – attack on wokeism, targeted hostility towards LGBTQ+ communities, migrants, and other marginalized groups. In making its argument regarding imperial continuity, the article applies Foucault’s concept of the ‘tyranny of discourse’ to show how imperia
items.title: Imperialism’s Modern Defenders and the Tyrannies of Discourse

items.abstract: Conventional-politics approaches, emphasizing party ideology, electoral dynamics, committee membership, campaign donations, and industry clout, exercise a powerful hold over assessments of public policies and their distributional effects. Emerging from pluralist and business power perspectives, such accounts see “who gets what and why” as the result of how politics and power shape policies, their implementation, and distributional outcomes. This pervades our understanding of the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), the US government’s effort to avert mass unemployment during the COVID-19 pandemic by lending $786 billion to small businesses to keep employees on the payroll. Yet contrary to prior studies of the PPP, we find that conventional-politics factors were strikingly uncorrelated with distributional outcomes, revealing limits to such approaches to this case. Instead, we find that an institutional politics or politics-in-time (IP-PIT) analysis better explains the program and its trajectories. IP-PIT revises the causal sequence by emphasizing how institutions and policies generate politics, distributional outcomes, and feedback loops. We engage both approaches via a mixed-methods
items.title: Business as Usual? Conventional Politics, Critical Junctures, and Policy Feedback in the Paycheck Protection Program

items.abstract: Debates on catastrophic artificial intelligence (AI) risk often frame artificial superintelligence as a problem of value alignment: the central task is to ensure that advanced systems act in accordance with human intentions or moral principles. This article argues that such a framing is necessary but insufficient. The danger posed by artificial superintelligence is not merely that it may pursue the wrong values, but that it may introduce a new concentration of autonomous and potentially dominating power. Drawing on political realism in both political theory and international relations, we reinterpret AI catastrophic risk as a structural problem of power under anarchy. The core concerns of AI safety—instrumental convergence, race dynamics, and loss of control—already rely on implicitly realist assumptions about survival, self-help, and the pursuit of power. Yet proposed solutions often retreat into moralism, asking states, firms, or machines to behave ethically without sufficiently altering the incentives that drive competitive acceleration. Against both moralistic reassurance and fatalistic resignation, we argue that realism offers a constructive response. Fear can coordinate divid
items.title: Fear, power, and superintelligence: A realist reframing of AI catastrophic risk

items.abstract: This article offers a new reading of decadence in Nietzsche, not as a time of despair or sclerosis, but as one of individuality and freedom. It does so by focusing on decadence’s emancipatory potential for exceptional individuals. For Nietzsche, the best philosophers, artists, and heroes do not merely emerge despite, but thanks to, decadence. Decadent times come with the collapse of institutions, conventions, and values—a self-destructive milieu that proves catastrophic for the many, but offers the possibility of emancipation for the few. I then show that some of Nietzsche’s core concepts are tied to this account of decadence, and suggest that Nietzsche’s view can offer a counterpoint to competing accounts of decadence from reactionary critics of modernity.
items.title: Nietzsche on Decadence as Freedom

items.abstract: Disagreement about democracy's noninstrumental value often sees the opposition between two competing approaches. Liberty‐based arguments assign normative priority to a principle of liberty, thereby focusing on democratic self‐government as the core principle through which political authority can be reconciled with individual liberty. Equality‐based arguments fundamentally appeal to equality instead, thus commending democratic procedures for treating citizens as equals in the decision‐making process. This paper targets Thomas Christiano's public equality argument for democracy, showing that its tacit reliance on a noncomparative norm of respect for the free and autonomous person leads it back to the liberty framework, as traditionally understood.
items.title: The Contested Grounds of Democracy's Noninstrumental Value: Deliberative Democracy Versus Public Equality

items.abstract: In a period marked by the inability of all variants of the Left to overcome the burden of defeat and fragmentation, of constant vacillations between reformism and sectarianism, this special issue of Historical Materialism attempts to reopen questions of strategy.
items.title: Special Issue on Strategy

items.abstract: Breaking carries many meanings, yet public life rarely lets it remain multiple: interruption is most often made legible only as damage awaiting repair. This article follows breaking through contemporary social movements to specify what a critical tradition descending from Foucault, Scott, and De Certeau leaves underarticulated, now that infrastructural systems are designed to anticipate and absorb disruption. Reading Alfred Sohn-Rethel’s account of Neapolitan tinkering, alongside Yuk Hui’s diagnosis of unbreakable technical ensembles, the argument situates breaking as world-making: a material politics over what is held together, what is relinquished, and at whose cost. Four contemporary repertoires – the No TAV movement, Soulèvements de la Terre , the looting of Black uprisings, and algorithmic poisoning – yield four recurring dimensions of breaking as intentionality, labour, temporality, and byproduction. Against repair’s moral economy, breaking emerges here as a diagnostic practice that prises open provisional futures where systems still give way.
items.title: Beyond Repair: Breaking as World-Making in Contemporary Social Movements

items.abstract: With the initial publication of his main economic work in 1859, Marx formulated his programme for an analysis of the bourgeois economy in the following order: capital, landed property, wage labour; state, foreign trade, world market. It was not until the 1920s and 1950s that Henryk Grossman and Roman Rosdolsky discussed whether the content of ‘Capital’ was based on a change in Marx’s structural plan. Important impulses for this discussion in the GDR , the FRG and the Soviet Union came in the following years from the advancing publication of the MEGA ² since 1976. We pay particular attention to the work of Wolfgang Jahn’s research group at the University of Halle. At the heart of this was and is the question of whether methodological and/or substantive breaks can be recognised in Marx’s critique of political economy that point to a change in his conceptions of planning. We deny this with reference to the continuity of his dialectical method of antithetical determination.
items.title: Structure and Method of the Critique of Political Economy: On the Debate over Marx’s Structural Plan – Part One

items.abstract: This essay intervenes in contemporary debates around neoliberalism and its relationship to both authoritarianism and social democracy. It does so by reconstructing the debate on Thatcherism that took place between Stuart Hall and Bob Jessop in the 1980s. Both authors provide materialist analyses of Thatcherism that point to important continuities, at the level of both political economy and authoritarian political technique, between her hegemonic project and late-stage social democracy. I argue that this provides an antidote to the social democratic nostalgia that is the potential product of the ways that neoliberalism is frequently theorised in the contemporary literature. While both thinkers highlight these continuities, they are more obviousin Jessop’s institutional approach to hegemony than in Hall’s analysis of Thatcher’s ideology.
items.title: The Origins of Neoliberal Authoritarianism: Hall and Jessop on the Crisis of Social Democracy and the Rise of Thatcher

items.abstract: Under neoliberalism, capitalist accumulation has become increasingly dependent on finance, including the financialisation of social reproduction. The centrality of finance to the reproduction of capital has been linked to both the global spread of informal and precarious forms of labour and the reconfiguration of state institutions according to the interests of finance capital. While the recomposition of capital, the working class, and the state has occurred unevenly, these processes have everywhere made the global working class more reliant on debt to ensure their own social reproduction, and these debt relations have become increasingly tied to the reproduction of finance capital. This paper demonstrates how, over the last several decades, intensified financialisation – defined as interest bearing capital ( IBC ) playing a key role in capitalist accumulation – has made both the reproduction of capital and the reproduction of the worker more dependent on finance, without displacing the pivotal role in accumulation played by value-producing wage labour.
items.title: Integrating Finance and Social Reproduction: Capital, Labour-Power, and Working-Class Formation

items.abstract: Social experiences of unfairness resist standard distributional accounts. This article argues that comparative relations do not merely shape responses to unequal outcomes but participate in constituting the sense of entitlement through which those outcomes are experienced as unfair. Drawing on René Girard’s social theory of mimetic desire, Leon Festinger’s social comparison theory, Axel Honneth’s account of recognition, and empirical research on inequity aversion from behavioural economics and comparative psychology, it develops a single mechanism—comparative entitlement formation—linking proximate comparison, the felt claim it generates, grievance, and, under determinate conditions, displacement onto vulnerable third parties. The argument is positioned between two literatures that approach the phenomenon from opposite directions and leave the same gap: egalitarian political philosophy has moved from the distribution of bundles toward the quality of social relations without supplying an account of how a comparative sense of entitlement is formed, while the recent literature on political grievance documents comparative resentment in detail without theorising the mechanism that gener
items.title: Comparative Desire and Social Violence: Mimetic Structure, Inequity, and the Scapegoat Dynamic

items.abstract: This article contributes to contemporary debates about racial capitalism by turning to Stuart Hall, a Jamaican cultural theorist active in the British New Left and the Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies. Hall made two moves to better diagnose the mediating role that “race” and racism played in the crises of post-war British capitalism. First, he adopted an imperial frame that situated Britain's industrialization in relation to its colonial sites of production. Second, Hall developed a “Marxism without final guarantees” that could explain how racialized difference becomes embedded within relations of production as a regulative norm. I argue his approach should be preferred to both formal and world-historical theories of racial capitalism, as the latter can fall back into an oversimplified economism. Hall's conjunctural analysis, by contrast, makes space for a more sustained consideration of both (a) the state and (b) a materialist account of popular culture.
items.title: Toward a conjunctural critique of racial capitalism

items.abstract: What makes a body of work ‘canonical’? In his writings over the years Jeffrey C. Alexander offers some phenomenologically convincing answers, each suggesting that the power of canonical texts is simultaneously context-immanent and context-transcending. However, a critical theory of ‘the canon’ cannot confine itself to phenomenological description. A critical theory is necessary due to the social constitution of the meanings of canonical texts. This gives rise to an endemic risk of ideological biases and the danger that canonization will reproduce and reinforce dominant perceptions of intellectual value, excluding or marginalizing authors and works who do not fit well with these perceptions. Accordingly, theories cognizant of this risk must explain the context-transcending component of the normativity of canonical works in a non-reductive way. This is a challenge for critical sociology.
items.title: Criticizing ‘the canon:’ A challenge for cultural sociology

items.abstract: This article argues that democratic double standards are not episodes of normative inconsistency but a mutable political technology for the differential distribution of legitimacy. The concept names a historically changing ensemble of institutional apparatuses, justificatory rationalities and material infrastructures through which the threshold of democratic legitimacy is unevenly allocated while its political function persists. It is distinguished from organised hypocrisy, ideology and discourse by four features: a function/mechanism distinction, institutional materiality, genealogical temporality and colonial asymmetry. The argument unfolds through a theory-generating genealogy organised around the Chile–Brazil axis – a historically dense dyad that condenses the technology in unusually legible form. Three moments of mutation are reconstructed: anti-communist destabilisation in Chile, the regionalisation of repression through Operation Condor and the reorganisation of political antagonism in Brazil. Integrating governmentality and the coloniality of power, it approaches Latin America as a theoretical archive for theorising the unevenness of democratic universalism.
items.title: Democratic double standards as a mutable political technology: A historical genealogy from Latin America

items.abstract: This contribution explores power and solidarity in Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology, bringing together his reflections on the social world in Phenomenology of Perception with his appraisal of sociology and Marxism in Signs and Adventures of the Dialectic . I argue that Merleau-Ponty reconfigures power as the crystallization of social interest that connects individuals and groups despite the differences in their social and political membership. This paves the way for a reconsideration of solidarity as the power to institute a different sense of reality from the shared experience of work and oppression. I conclude with an illustration of the contingency of solidarity in connection with the social struggle that led to the Italian law 199/2016 against the exploitation of undocumented workers.
items.title: Power and solidarity in Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology

items.abstract: Louis Althusser shows how interpellation functions as a mechanism for the constituting of subjects delineated through ideology. While Althusser focuses his analysis on verbal interpellation, critical theorists have shown that interpellation need not be limited to vocative hails. In this article, I show how one can interpellate with their bodily motility, comportment, and even physiological functions. In particular, I argue that racist ideologies can become naturalized onto bodies in such a way that individuals can interpellate racialized others as inhabiting inferior social positions. Racist embodied interpellations call racialized subjects to see themselves occupying stereotypical images which can fundamentally impact identity shaping processes. However, it is not the case that this subject formation is ontologically totalizing. Rather, embodied interpellations can cause the hailed racialized subject to confront the conflict between their own self-image and the dominant stereotypical perception of them. Quill Kukla offers a systematic overview of interpellation and describes two features of a successful interpellation. I utilize a concrete example that illustrates the importance o
items.title: Embodied Interpellation: Racist Bodily Interactions and Racialized Subject Formation

items.abstract: This paper proposes a reconstruction of Sartre’s ontology of interpersonal relations organized around the concept of recognition. It begins with Honneth’s critique of Sartre, taking it as an opportunity to clarify the distinctive character of Sartre’s ontological approach to recognition. Central to this approach is the idea that a tension exists between intersubjective intimacy and existential separation, which Sartre regards as constitutive of the self-other relation. His analysis of this tension hinges on the concept of original recognition, as embodied in our affective response to the look of the Other. This recognition, however, is inherently ambiguous. While attesting to an original generosity of our interpersonal relations, it is also the source of potential conflict – a conflict that need not be perpetual but can be constructively overcome.
items.title: Sartre on the Ambiguity of Recognition

items.abstract: This paper examines Jacques Derrida’s and Gillian Rose’s conceptions of “home” as an ambiguous realm between belonging and estrangement, rootedness and displacement. Both resist simple accounts of home as a stable refuge or secure place of origin, yet they differ in how they respond to its incompleteness. For Derrida, home is shaped by fear of dissolution and loss—loss of belonging, collapse of the safety that makes dwelling possible. This fear gives home a “spectral” quality, visible in the aporetic structure of hospitality and in the terror of linguistic homelessness. Rose, drawing on Hegelian speculative identity, understands home as a process of mediation, formed through the ongoing work of negotiating contradictions in the present. Through readings of texts from the 1980s and 1990s, this paper argues that their different orientations toward fear and mediation yield distinct ethical and political visions. Derrida’s “messianic without messianism” sustains the promise of justice precisely by refusing to settle it within a determinate order. Rose’s “inaugurated mourning,” by contrast, wagers that transformation remains possible through engagement with the “broken middle” of actual
items.title: Jacques Derrida, Gillian Rose, and the question of home
